title: Distributed Rate Limiting
description: Implement distributed rate limiting across multiple API gateway instances using Redis cluster, sticky sessions, and consistent hashing.

data.text: In a distributed system with multiple API gateway instances, rate limit state must be shared. In-memory rate limiters fail because each instance has its own counter. You need a shared store — typically Redis — and a strategy to keep it consistent under high concurrency.

cards.title: Centralized Redis
cards.description: All gateways read/write rate limit state to a single Redis cluster.
cons: Redis is a single point of failure
Redis cluster sharding must consider rate limit key distribution

cards.title: Sticky Sessions
cards.description: Route the same client to the same gateway instance for rate limiting.
cons: Breaks on instance restart or scale-down
Client failover resets their rate limit

cards.title: Consistent Hashing
cards.description: Hash the rate limit key to a specific gateway instance.

data.text: Use a Redis Cluster with the rate limit key as the hash tag. Lua scripts run atomically on the shard that owns the key. This gives you a single source of truth with sub-millisecond latency.

data.title: Redis Cluster key design for rate limiting
data.content: Use hash tags to ensure all rate limit keys for a user land on the same shard.
data.code:
# Redis Cluster hash tag: {user:123}
# All keys with the same tag hash to the same shard

KEYS:
  {user:123}:rate:tokens    # Token balance for user 123
  {user:123}:rate:last      # Last refill timestamp
  {user:123}:sliding:prev   # Sliding window previous count
  {user:123}:sliding:curr   # Sliding window current count

# Lua script runs on the shard that owns {user:123}
# All operations are atomic — no race conditions across shards

data.title: Envoy gRPC rate limit service configuration
data.content: Envoy delegates rate limiting to a gRPC service that queries Redis.
data.code:
# Envoy rate limit config
extension_config:
  name: envoy.rate_limit_descriptors

rate_limits:
  - actions:
      - generic_key:
          descriptor_key: user_id
          value: "%REQ:x-user-id%"
  - actions:
      - generic_key:
          descriptor_key: endpoint
          value: "%REQ(:path)%"

# Rate limit service (RLS) gRPC backend
rate_limit_service:
  grpc_service:
    envoy_grpc:
      cluster_name: rate_limit_cluster
  transport_api_version: V3

# RLS checks Redis via Lua and returns:
# OK: allow request
# OVER_LIMIT: reject with 429

items: Use Redis Cluster with replicas for high availability
If Redis is unreachable, decide: fail open (allow all) or fail closed (reject all)
Most production APIs fail open — a rate limit outage should not take down the entire API
Alert on Redis latency spikes; a slow Redis degrades all rate limit decisions
Use sentinel or cluster auto-failover for automatic Redis recovery

rows: Use hash tags to keep related keys on same shard
Cache results locally with short TTL

data.title: The distributed penalty
data.text: Distributed rate limiting adds 1-3ms of latency per request. For APIs with strict latency budgets (<10ms), consider local rate limiting with periodic Redis sync, or accept that rate limiting requires a latency tax.

items.question: Can I use PostgreSQL instead of Redis?
items.answer: PostgreSQL can work but is slower for high-throughput rate limiting. Use it for billing or compliance where accuracy matters more than throughput. Use Redis for real-time API rate limiting.

items.question: How do I prevent Redis hot shards?
items.answer: Use consistent hash tags and avoid high-cardinality keys hitting the same shard. Distribute rate limit keys across the cluster using a prefix like rate:{hash(userId) % 16}:{userId}.

items.question: Should I use a CDN for rate limiting?
items.answer: CDNs can rate limit at the edge, but they lack the granularity of per-user Redis state. Use CDN rate limiting for IP-based abuse prevention and Redis for authenticated user quotas.

data.title: Key takeaway
points: Centralized Redis with Lua scripts is the standard distributed pattern.
Hash tags keep related keys on the same Redis shard.
Fail open on Redis outages — rate limiting should not cause downtime.
Add 1-3ms latency budget for the Redis round-trip.
data.takeaway: Distributed rate limiting is a solved problem with Redis. The hard part is not the algorithm — it is handling Redis failures gracefully and keeping key distribution even across the cluster.
